title: Knowledge units teach something new
statement: Count a unit as building knowledge only when it teaches something about the world learners don't already know; familiar themes such as family or pets give practice, not knowledge.
detail: A pedagogy red team on a second-grade reading plan found that its knowledge units, re-scoped to themes drawn from the passages it reused, such as family and friends, nature, animals and pets and everyday life, build essentially no new background knowledge: a child gains no new schema from another story about a family or a pet (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/redteam-2-pedagogy.md`, lines 74-80). It grounds this in the knowledge thesis, which asks courses to teach children what they don't yet know about the world so that later texts on those topics are comprehensible, and calls the themed units comprehension practice on familiar content: fine, but not knowledge-first (the same file, line 80). The narrowed plan that followed made no knowledge-building claim (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/optionB-prime-narrow-rebuild.md`).

evidence.quote: "family/friends 92, nature/outdoors 65, building/making 57, animals/pets 41, everyday life 32, adventure 17."
A child gains no new schema from another story about a family or a pet. So the "Knowledge Expeditions," as re-scoped to corpus themes, **build essentially no new background knowledge**
*teach children what they don't yet know about the world (the water cycle, ancient Rome, insects) so that future texts on those topics are comprehensible.*
they are comprehension *practice* on familiar content, which is fine, but it is not "knowledge-first"
